btos.label: Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction (NAICS 21)

name: Mining
blurb: Autonomous haulage and ore-body modelling in the sector that automated early, from USGS exploration data and Earth MRI to Rio Tinto, Komatsu, KoBold, and the AI-native explorers.

points.desc: Census BTOS reports mining-sector AI use directly from firms.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The Mineral Resources Program is the public record of US mineral assessments - the satellite, geophysical, and historical data that exploration models train on.
points.name: USGS anchors the exploration data layer

points.desc: The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative is systematically re-mapping US geology with modern geophysics - the dataset behind machine-learning prospectivity work on critical minerals.
points.name: Earth MRI maps the country for critical minerals

points.desc: The company's own automation program - autonomous haul trucks and drills operating at scale - is the primary-source record of what day-to-day operational AI looks like in production mining.
points.name: Rio Tinto runs the operations proof point

points.desc: One of the two dominant mining-equipment makers publishes its autonomous haulage and fleet-management technology - where operational AI ships as machinery.
points.name: Komatsu documents the autonomous equipment layer

points.desc: The National Mining Association tracks regulatory change and technology adoption across American mining operations - the sector's US policy layer.
points.name: NMA is the US trade association

points.desc: The International Council on Mining and Metals tracks ESG standards, automated safety monitoring, and digital transformation across the major international operators.
points.name: ICMM sets the global operator standards

points.desc: The Society for Mining, Metallurgy & Exploration publishes the working-group research on AI, machine learning, and automation in mineral processing.
points.name: SME carries the technical research

points.desc: The AI-first exploration company applies machine learning and geospatial modelling to target battery-metal deposits - lithium, cobalt, copper, nickel - and is the sector's clearest AI-native bet.
points.name: KoBold Metals is the AI-native explorer

points.desc: The US copper major applies machine-learning models to processing - maximizing mill throughput and ore recovery at existing operations rather than finding new ones.
points.name: Freeport-McMoRan optimizes the mill with ML

points.desc: The major gold miners use AI for drill-core analysis, predictive maintenance, and automated safety monitoring - Newmont's and Barrick's own technology pages are the record.
points.name: Barrick and Newmont apply AI to gold

points.desc: Computer-vision core scanning (GeologicAI) and real-time ore characterization at the mine face (Plotlogic) - the specialist vendors turning geology into a machine-readable input.
points.name: GeologicAI and Plotlogic scan the rock itself

summary: Autonomous haulage and ore-body modelling are the established deployments in a sector that adopted automation early. Mining AI splits into two horizons: exploration - long-term forecasting from satellite, magnetic, and core-scan data toward drilling targets - and site operations, where sensor streams and telemetry drive machinery, maintenance, and safety minute by minute.

analysis.body:
About 7.2 percent of mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction firms reported using AI in the most recent Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey period, down slightly from 7.9 percent in the prior period. That modest figure sits against a sector that is often cited as an early automation adopter, which suggests that large-operator deployments visible in the headlines are not yet representative of the broader industry. The gap between what the major producers have built and what the average firm is running is one of the defining features of the current moment.

The documented uses concentrate in two distinct zones. Operational AI centers on autonomous haulage and drilling equipment, where Rio Tinto's at-scale programs and Komatsu's fleet-management systems represent the clearest production-grade evidence of what day-to-day deployment looks like. Mill optimization is the other proven application, with Freeport-McMoRan applying machine-learning models to copper processing to lift throughput and ore recovery at existing sites. Barrick and Newmont extend the pattern into gold mining through predictive maintenance, drill-core analysis, and automated safety monitoring. On the exploration side, KoBold Metals applies machine learning and geospatial modelling to target battery-metal deposits, while specialist vendors GeologicAI and Plotlogic translate physical rock into machine-readable inputs through computer-vision core scanning and real-time ore characterization at the mine face. The public data layer underneath much of this exploration work flows from the USGS Mineral Resources Program and the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, which is systematically re-mapping US geology for critical-mineral prospectivity.

The risk and standards picture is carried primarily by the International Council on Mining and Metals, which tracks ESG commitments, automated safety monitoring, and digital transformation across the major international operators, and by the National Mining Association on the US regulatory side. Safety monitoring is both a genuine use case and a compliance lever, since automated systems can generate auditable records that support the reporting obligations operators already face. The Society for Mining, Metallurgy and Exploration publishes the technical research underpinning these deployments, meaning the knowledge base is reasonably well-documented even where commercial disclosure is thin.

A reader weighing deployment should take away that the strongest returns documented so far come from applying AI to assets already in production, specifically mill optimization and predictive maintenance, rather than from exploration alone. Autonomous haulage delivers measurable cost and safety outcomes but requires the capital footprint that only the largest operators carry. For smaller firms, the more accessible entry points are the specialist scanning and ore-characterization vendors, which slot into existing workflows without requiring a full equipment overhaul. The overall adoption rate suggests most operations have not yet made that move, which means competitive differentiation is still available but so is the option of watching larger operators refine the playbook before committing.
